newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Hillary, Chelsea see splendor of Victoria Falls.
newsitem.headline: Hillary, Chelsea see splendor of Victoria Falls.

text.p: U.S. First Lady Hillary Rodham Clinton and daughter Chelsea savoured the surging splendor of Victoria Falls on Sunday and got wet from the spray that shot high overhead.
"Wow, great, it's great," President Clinton's wife said as she stood on a cliff overlook spot and watched the Zambezi River tumbling 300 feet into a gorge hidden by a thick cloud of roaring spray.

In the Kololo language, the falls are known as the "Moisi- Oa-Tunya" -- the Smoke that Thunders, and the cloud it produces can be seen for miles, and indeed was watched by those aboard the first lady's airplane as it flew to Victoria Falls from Harare.
It was in this natural beauty that Clintons chose to do some sightseeing on Palm Sunday after a week of mostly business during their two-week tour of Africa.
They walked about a mile along a trail through a rain forest that feeds from the spray and lingered at overlook spots along the way with names such as "the Devil's Cataract," or "Cataract Island."
Umbrellas gave them only partial protection and both Mrs. Clinton and her 17-year-old daughter got soaked.
At one point mother and daughter cupped their ears with heads tilted toward the falls to listen to the pure roar, on the advice of guide Glenn Tatham, chief warden for Zimbabwe's national parks.
"If you cup your ears like that you can hear the energy," Mrs. Clinton said.
Tatham said: "It's a very romantic thing to come here on a full moon and see a lunar rainbow."
Indeed rainbows were spotted in the gorge throughout the falls, which measure nearly a mile across and are considered one of the wonders of the world, much larger than America's Niagara Falls.
"Did you all see the rainbow. Can you take a picture of the rainbow?" Mrs. Clinton told photographers.
"Work with her. Don't tip her over," said Mrs. Clinton's spokesman, Neel Lattimore, when the photographers surged forward.
The spray surges back up into the air and falls with every appearance of raindrops, an odd sensation with blue sky and puffy white clouds overhead.
"No, Mom," protested Chelsea when her mother wanted to keep the umbrella above her head while being photographed. The umbrella was put aside.
At one overlook Mrs. Clinton was standing on some slick rocks and looking at a vividly coloured rainbow in the gorge far below, prompting one Secret Service agent to hold her arm in case she slipped.
At the end of the tour Mrs. Clinton and Chelsea watched someone go bungee-jumping from the centre of Victoria Falls bridge, a span that separates Zimbabwe from Zambia.
The jumper fell a long way, bounced around and then was brought back up.
"Oh goodness," said U.S. ambassador to Zimbabwe, Johnnie Carson.
"What's it like?" Mrs. Clinton asked one fellow who told her what it was like.
"Oy," was her cautious reply.
